title: Federal Agents Search Ilhan Omar's Washington Home Under Court-Authorized Warrant
excerpt: The Justice Department said Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorised warrant on October 12 as part of an ongoing investigation. Omar denies wrongdoing, no charges have been reported, and she called the search an attempt to target political enemies.
body:
• Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C. home on Monday morning, October 12, under a judicially authorised warrant the Justice Department said it approved.
  • The Justice Department said the search was part of an ongoing federal investigation and gave no further public details; no charges have been reported.
  • Officials speaking anonymously linked the search to a multi-year probe involving whistleblower complaints and immigration-fraud allegations, which Omar denies.
  • Readers should treat the allegations as unproven: a search warrant is not a charge, and Omar is seeking reelection in next month's midterm elections.

Federal agents searched the Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, the Minnesota Democrat, on Monday morning, October 12. The Department of Justice told NPR that agents with Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorised search warrant. The department said the warrant was approved by the Justice Department and was part of an ongoing federal investigation, and it gave no further details about the reason for the probe.

Al Jazeera described the search the same way, as part of an undisclosed criminal investigation, and noted that it came just weeks before the midterm elections, after years of attacks on Omar from President Donald Trump and Republicans.

What officials have said, and what is not known

Details beyond the Justice Department statement came from current and former federal officials who spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly. One current official said the search was part of a multi-year probe that includes whistleblower complaints. A former official who had previously been briefed on the matter said the investigation deals with immigration-fraud allegations.

https://x.com/FoxNews/status/2109621969524068612

Those allegations are unproven. No charges have been reported in connection with the search, federal authorities have not said publicly what they were looking for, and a warrant by itself is not an accusation of a crime. Vice President JD Vance has previously alleged that Omar committed immigration fraud. Omar denies that allegation, and she has denied wrongdoing more broadly. USA Today reported that other senior administration officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have also made that allegation over time, which she denies.

Neighbour Sharon Jackson, 79, who lives across the street, told NPR that agents woke her at about 4:30 a.m. on Monday and that a large truck was outside. Several Homeland Security Investigations agents were seen walking near and around the home during the morning.

Omar's response

Omar responded on social media: "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. I will not be silenced."

Her spokesperson, Jackie Rogers, called the search an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponisation of federal law enforcement against political opponents. Omar also characterised the search to USA Today as the latest step in a campaign of political intimidation. House Democratic leadership, including Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, called the search deeply disturbing in a joint statement and pointed to the timing, less than 30 days before the midterm election.

Why the timing and the case matter

Omar, first elected in 2018 and the first Somali American in Congress, was born in Somalia and came to the United States as a child refugee, according to USA Today. She is seeking reelection in next month's midterms. The search therefore lands in the final weeks of a campaign, involving a sitting member of Congress who is also one of the most prominent immigrant lawmakers in the country.

For immigrant communities, the factual position is narrower than the political argument around it. A high-profile search connected, according to anonymous officials, to immigration-fraud allegations can raise anxiety well beyond one household, even when no charges have been filed and the target denies wrongdoing. The reliable record at this stage consists of the Justice Department's short public statement, Omar's public response, and reporting attributed to named and anonymous officials. Anything beyond that remains allegation, not a finding.

What happens next

The Justice Department has described the investigation as ongoing and has not announced charges, further searches or a timetable. Omar's office has said she will not be silenced, and she remains a candidate in the midterm elections. Further information, if it comes, is likely to come through court filings, a fuller Justice Department statement, or Omar's office, rather than through speculation about the anonymous allegations reported so far.
